blocks.text: If someone curses you, beat him until he gives in; if someone shows you a look of disgust, question that damned bastard. The illusion breaks, reality returns, and you drift through the remaining fifty-odd years until death takes me home. Pick up your hunting rifle, and you'll never hear the cursing again.
It's tiring, sure, but you'll get something out of it. Why not tell me what you want? You'll be crushed by reality anyway.
If dissociation is pulling the handbrake, anti-dissociation is stepping on the gas.

The NMDA receptor is agonized, perception is passed to cognition in large amounts, and perception and cognition are strengthened together. Metaphorically, anti-dissociation is pressure and acceleration. You can finally observe every detail: seeing reality clearly is a rise in cognition. Memory and learning are strengthened, smell and taste are strengthened — umami is transmitted by NMDA; MSG is monosodium glutamate, and glutamate makes food taste savoury. Depersonalization is treated back the other way.
But with the gas floored, the engine burns.

In a car, agonizing NMDA is stepping on the gas, antagonizing it is pulling the handbrake. With heavy dissociation the car doesn't move, the engine is intact, even seemingly protected; with heavy anti-dissociation the car flies, the engine works violently, overworks, wears, cracks. In the end the ruined engine stops working too, and the car goes back to not moving. This is excitotoxicity: calcium floods in, osmotic pressure shifts, nerve cells swell with water and burst and die. The death of nerve cells is irreversible, far more terrifying than 'not letting the receptor work'.
So anti-dissociation is a double-edged drug, and which way the edge points depends on whether the user has enough psychological energy.

Dissociation protects a powerless self from being exposed to pain; anti-dissociation lets a powerful self understand the pain, so as to judge how to solve it. Dissociation satisfies the wish to be spared pain; if a dissociated person is forcibly anti-dissociated, that person begins to bear the pain. For the powerful this is exactly the beginning of a solution; for the powerless it is a form of abuse.

Whether it's depression or antidepressant, anxiety or anxiolytic, the key lies in the user's own agency. Dissociation makes people anxious because it keeps them from cognizing where the anxiety comes from — like an invisible person hitting you all the time; anti-dissociation makes people anxious because it makes them cognize that the anxiety exists — like seeing how many people are hitting you. Seeing who's hitting you is the beginning of a solution — provided you can win, or can run.
This is why some ask: anti-dissociatives strengthen cognition, but there's a catch — what if, after strengthening cognition, you see your own predicament even more clearly?
